messages.subject: batch procedures
messages.body_plain:
Dear list,

I've developed a SAS procedure to bootstrap a  distance survey at different
levels of effort.
The procedure generate a large file (58760 records) and Distance 5.0 spent
about 13 hours to charge the data (step 6 of the wizard) which is a bit
boring. So I tried to execute distance in batch mode (with the hope it may
run faster) using the procedure generated by Distance itself and changing
appropriately the infile statement. As a first step in my learning I
executed a much shorter file in mode "debug" so that I obtained suitable
data input  and procedure files. When in Windows XP, I run a file .bat with
the following istructions:

D:\TESI\prova_import\MCDS.exe 0,dstF2.tmp
pause

where dstF2.tmp is the istructions file generated by distance appropiately
corrected for the input data file.
Every time MCDS generates 4 as output and stops. I've tried also with a
combination of " " as shown in the Distance book and also without using a
procedure but excuting directly the program MCDS.EXE. I've checked previous
answers on the list but I was unable to track the problem. Where am I wrong?

Thanks for your help,

Stefano

messages.subject: Re: information on platform design
messages.body_plain:
Nino-

I suggest that you read section 6.10 of the Advanced Distance Sampling
book if you have not already done so.  While it does not completely
answer your question it does address some issues that you are asking
about.  The answer to your questions depends on the species and what you
are trying to accomplish.  I presume that what you are trying to do is
use the secondary observer to set up trial detections for the primary
observer to estimate detection probability that is unaffected by
potential movement of cetaceans and to assess availability bias.  The
answer of how "high" for the secondary observer depends on how far away
you can see the cetaceans, how far away you expect that they may respond
(if at all) to the vessel and what their average dive times are.  For
movement you want the secondary observer to detect them before they
respond and for availability bias(diving) you want the time between
possible detections of primary and secondary to exceed the length of the
average dive interval.

"which ones could be the benefits/disavantages in not keeping to or
observing it?"
I'm not certain what you mean by the above.  If you are asking is it
worth doing a secondary observer, that will again depend on the species
you are surveying and how likely responsive movement will occur and
whether detection probability will be close to 1.

Much of this is species specific.  I suggest that you do a thorough
literature search for papers about surveys and survey techniques for the
species you are interested in.

regards --jeff laake

messages.subject: Re: batch procedures
messages.body_plain:
Dear Tiago, Len, list,

thanks for your help. Now it's working. From the last 24-hours experience I
can add 2 points which can be useful to novices like me:

1) it also works if you  copy the file mcds.exe in the working directory
2) in the input file you have to list all output files potentially useful to
DISTANCE before the "options;" subcommand (names are of fantasy)

like

out.txt
log.txt
stat.txt
boot.txt
plot.txt
ris.txt
Options;

In such a way they are written in the working directory.

Cheers,

Stefano

----- Original Message -----
From: "Distance Development" <dist...@mcs.st-and.ac.uk>
To: "Stefano Dott. Focardi" <stefano...@INFS.IT>
Sent: Tuesday, May 09, 2006 4:40 PM
Subject: Re: [DIST-SAMP] batch procedures

> > Stefano, list,
> >
> > Tiago is right, it's the missing space that is critical

> > D:\TESI\prova_import\MCDS.exe 0,dstF2.tmp

> > will not work
> > D:\TESI\prova_import\MCDS.exe 0, dstF2.tmp
> > will.
> >
> > I have altered the manual so it makes this clear (by adding a note to the
> > relevant page - see below).
> >
> > I'm sorry that importing takes so long in D5 - I'm hoping to have a
> > significantly faster version (but with less functionality) available as a
> > complement by the next release.
> >
> > Cheers,
> >
> > - Len
> >
> > Page from the manual (MCDS appendix):
> > ---------------------------
> > Running the MCDS engine
> >
> > The command to run the MCDS engine is
> > MCDS Parameter1, Parameter2
> > where
> > Parameter1 is either a 0 or a 1.  0 is for run mode - i.e. run the
> > analysis.
> > 1 is for import mode, which is used to implement part of the Project
> > Import
> > feature in Distance and is not described further here.
> > Parameter2 is the filename of the input command file - see MCDS Command
> > Language, below for details of the contents of this file.
> >
> > Example 1:
> > Assume that we have a command window open in the Distance program
> > directory
> > (usually C:\Program Files\Distance5), and that we have a file
> > TestInput.txt
> > in that directory.  Then we type:
> > MCDS 0, TestInput.txt
> >
> > Example 2:
> > Assume we have a command window open in some arbitrary directory (e.g., C:
> > \).  Assume that we have an input command file C:\Temp\Input File.txt that
> > we want to run.  Assume that the MCDS.exe program is in the Distance
> > program
> > directory C:\Program Files\Distance5.  Because both the input file and the
> > Distance program directory have spaces in them, we need to enclose the
> > program and file names in quotes:
> > "C:\Program Files\Distance5\MCDS" 0, "C:\Temp\Input File.txt"
> >
> > Note. The space between MCDS and parameter 1, and the space and comma
> > between parameter 1 and parameter 2 are critical.  For example, in Example
> > 1, above,
> > MCDS 0,TestInput.txt
> > will not work (it will return the value 4 - file error) because there is
> > no
> > space between parameter 1 and parameter 2.
> >
> > Tip. An example of how to run the MCDS analysis engine from a program
> > written in another language (in this case Visual Basic) is given on the
> > Support page of the Program Distance Web Site.  See also the archives of
> > the
> > Distance-sampling Email List for some messages discussing how to do this
> > (try searching for "stand alone").
> > ---------------------------
> >
> >
> > --
> > Len Thomas, Co-ordinator, Distance Development Project
> > Research Unit for Wildlife Population Assessment
> > Centre for Research into Environmental and Ecological Modelling
> > The Observatory, University of St Andrews, Scotland KY16 9LZ
> >
> >             email: dist...@mcs.st-and.ac.uk
> > Distance home page: http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distance/

> >

messages.body_plain:
Dear list,

We are currently conducting a research in an urban park in Israel.

Using the distance procedure we conducted point sampling of birds.

Sampling was done using 10 meter belts from 0 to 50 meters (5 belts).
Because of practical reasons sampling of birds from 50 meters to 100 meters
were grouped together.

We are now attempting to use the Distance Program and are faced with a
dilemma.

How should we represent the data obtained in the last belt?

Obviously different representation of the data greatly affect the estimation
of density.

Thank you

Assaf SHwartz

messages.subject: more distance sampling references
messages.body_plain:
Dear list,

The webpage with pdf's of papers and reports related to
distance sampling that I keep online at

http://www.creem.st-and.ac.uk/tiago/webpages/distance_pdfs.htm

has reached more than 100 references, with over 5000 visits since it
started. Thanks for those who have contributed for it.

I've decided to put online a new bibliographic list on distance
sampling, available at

http://www.creem.st-and.ac.uk/tiago/webpages/distbiblio.html

It contains over 600 references on work done with or about distance
sampling (important: these are not online as pdf's; in fact, I've not
yet combined the two lists, i.e., there might be papers online as pdf's
that I have not included in the new reference list - a TO DO for the
future,). If you happen to
look at it, please let me know if you have any suggestions, new entries,
corrections for existing ones, etc.

In such a large amount of references it is likely that there might be
some errors (in the next weeks I'll probably correct many minor typos
etc), so double check any info you use from it - I take no
responsibility for it's use.

It is not a complete list, but references
I've collected from several sources and also as result of my own web
searching activities.

For those of you with new PhD, MSc, etc students in topics related to
distance sampling, this might be a good way of introducing them to the
bibliography in the area. If you do so, please tell your students to
contact me if they find any errors or mistakes.

A note about the hiperlinks on the new bibliographic list page: they are
dead, and just a nuisance, resulting from the conversion from TeX to
HTML. If someone knows how to deal with it I would greatly apreciate a hi=
nt.

I hope this might be helpful to some of you. If it is, let me know...
it's always good to know.

Tiago

messages.subject: Line transects for sparrows
messages.body_plain:
Distance lovers:
    I'm working up protocol for surveying breeding Henslow Sparrows in
Tennessee.  They are secretive grassland birds, but sing regularly and
can be surveyed adequately with line transects.  I have several fields
where they breed, but I have a technical problem I have to deal with in
order to conduct surveys without violating assumptions of distance
sampling.  The main problem is that some fields are narrow (~50m or
less), where we can only do one-sided transects where we walked the
transect line as the edge between mowed and unmowed habitat.  I'm ok
with one-sided transects.  I think I can deal with surveying narrow
habitats.
   To build up to the question, I think I'm going to run a series of
one-sided transects at our 3 sites, which will deal with the narrow
habitat issue.  The problem is that 2 large fields (300m x ~400m) have a
lot of firebreaks mowed lengthwise thru the field.  Essentially there
are several 15-25m wide strips of "suitable" habitat (with standing dead
native warm season grasses) that stretch the length of the field and
then there's a 10m wide strip of growing blackberry and other greenery
not so suitable for Henslow's, repeat for 300m.  I'm sure HESP's forage
in the greenery/firebreaks, but would not necessarily use it for
nesting.  To add to the plot, HESP's are found in large fields of almost
exclusively green grasses that were burned the previous year (not
expected to be optimal habitat).  So maybe the firebreaks aren't really
a series issue.  My question is how to deal with the firebreaks and
unsuitable nesting habitat scattered between lines of suitable habitat?
Doing a point count isn't really the way to go for surveying these guys,
but a line transect would survey ample suitable and unsuitable habitat,
thus on a given transect, there would never be detections from 15-25m on
the length of the transect.  Also, if we worked line transects, walking
the edge of the mowed/ummowed grasses would be best, but I'm not sure if
we violate assumptions of distance sampling because there may be no HESP
along the transect line.  Thus we would technically get all the birds
along the line, but that is because there may not be any.

Thoughts would be greatly appreciated.

Thanks,
Scott Somershoe

State Ornithologist
Tennessee Wildlife Resources Agency
P.O. Box 40747
Nashville, TN 37204
615-781-6653 (o)
601-868-0101 (cell)
615-781-6654 (fax)

"Keeping the rubber side down." -SGS

I wonder if it is possible to put lines perpendicular to these features?
If necessary, cut a narrow strip, cutting across the habitat types.  That
way, habitat type won't be correlated with distance from the line.

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: Re: Line transects for sparrows
messages.body_plain:
Scott,

I think Steve's suggestion to run your transects perpendicular to the
habitat strips is what you have to do.  Even though only the warm-season
grasses are the nesting habitat, the birds are using the firebreaks as
well and I think you have to treat the whole area as habitat to be
surveyed.  This is likely the preferred approach for the mowed/unmowed
areas as well.

I also have some other comments relevant to distance sampling and this
species.  I have been using distance sampling to survey grassland
sparrows (Henslow's, grasshopper, and Savannah) for a number of years
and it works quite well.  However, we only estimate the number of
visible, singing males because you need a song to distinguish among
species at longer sighting distances, and you need a visual sighting to
measure accurate distances.  Their song is just too ventriloquistic to
estimate distance from auditory detection.

However, by limiting oneself to only visible, singing males your
estimate of density is biased low by the proportion of time birds are
not singing or visible.  I have called this an 'availability' issue in
that only about 40% of Henslow's males are visible and singing during a
line transect survey - and distance sampling assumes all birds are
available for detection.  I and my colleagues  have a paper accepted for
publication in The Auk (January '07) that discusses this issue and
estimates the availability.  The good news is that this availability for
Henslow's sparrows did not appear to change during mid-May through June
(unlike grasshopper sparrows) but I can't guarantee our estimates for
Pennsylvania would be the same in Tennesee.  But at least you could
argue that this availability issue results in your density estimates
being biased low, and that this bias may be constant.

If you have any further questions feel free to contact me.

Regards,

Duane Diefenbach
